identity.title: Learning to Search from Demonstration Sequences

problem.claim: Learn search and planning from action-observation sequences such as demonstrations or instructions when other learning signals are unavailable.

gap.claim: The abstract reports that relying only on supervised learning from such sequences can be sub-optimal because training encounters a vast unseen search space.

contributions.claim: Introduces D-TSN, a neural architecture that learns to construct search trees from demonstration sequences by differentiating through best-first tree construction.
Jointly learns planning components—an encoder, value function, and world model—and models stochastic tree expansion as a decision-making task optimized with REINFORCE plus variance reduction.
Supports settings with either a known world model or a jointly learned latent-state world model.

stated_novelty.claim: The authors describe D-TSN as a novel architecture for learning search-tree construction from demonstration sequences through gradient descent on a best-first search algorithm.

author_reported_evidence.claim: The authors report experiments on Game of 24, 2D grid navigation, and Procgen games spanning known-model and jointly learned latent-state-model settings.
The authors report that D-TSN is effective, particularly when the latent-state world model is jointly learned.

narrative_sequence.summary: Search and planning matter for real-world problem solving, but learning may provide only demonstrations or instruction sequences.
Sequence-only supervised learning may struggle with the unseen search space encountered during training.
D-TSN differentiates through best-first tree construction and jointly learns key planning modules.
Stochastic tree expansion is treated as a decision problem and optimized with REINFORCE using variance reduction.
Experiments cover three task domains and report particular benefit in jointly learned latent-state world-model settings.

source_observation.claim: The abstract links the learning-signal constraint, the unseen-search-space limitation, and a method that explicitly differentiates through search-tree construction.

lessons.interpretation: A paper can make its methodological motivation more concrete by aligning the proposed mechanism with the identified failure mode.
lessons.application: When proposing a planning method from demonstrations, explicitly state which search operation is learned or differentiated and how that operation addresses sequence-only supervision.
lessons.exception: This framing is less suitable when the main contribution concerns representation learning or tasks without an explicit search process.

unknowns: No quantitative results, baselines, statistical details, or task-specific conditions are provided, so the strength and scope of the reported effectiveness cannot be assessed.
The abstract does not specify which components or settings drive the reported advantage beyond emphasizing jointly learned latent-state world models.
